Hook: In 2016 four economists, Abel Brodeur, Mathias Lé, Marc Sangnier and Yanos Zylberberg, did something simple. They collected fifty thousand test statistics from three of the most prestigious journals in economics, everything published between 2005 and 2011, and drew their distribution. If journals printed whatever researchers found, that distribution would be smooth. It was not. There was a valley where results are close to significant but not quite, p-values between a quarter and a tenth. And a bump just past the line of statistical significance, the famous five percent. They estimated that between a tenth and a fifth of the results that just clear the line should have fallen short of it. Results that were nearly significant had gone somewhere.

This series cannot reach into those journals' files, but it can build a field in which the truth is known. A hundred and sixty thousand studies, each with a true effect, which for three in ten is exactly zero. Each researcher runs a first analysis. If it is not significant, some try other reasonable specifications and report the first that works. Journals then publish every significant result and about a third of the rest. Here is what gets published, 91,504 results. The camel's valley and its bump are both there. And here, in blue, is what the same studies found on their first try, rescaled to the same total: smooth, no valley, no bump. Just above the line against just below it, the published results run 3.2 to one; the first tries, 0.9 to one. In this field we know exactly where the bump comes from, because we built it: from researchers who search and journals that select.

Sixty-six parts have told you what economics says. This one asks how much of it is true. How often do published results replicate, and can you tell in advance which ones will? How do search and selection bend a literature, and can we correct for them? What changed when economics turned from theory to data? What do its models leave out, and who decides what gets published? And what will machines change about how economists find things out?
Economics, Built. Part sixty-seven: the next economics.

Part sixty-six asked what states do with trade. This part turns the series' tools on economics itself. By the end you will know what the large replication projects found, and why replicated effects are smaller; how to see specification search and publication bias in a literature, and how to correct for them; what pre-analysis plans, registered reports and multiple-testing rules can and cannot do; how the field turned empirical, why many analysts on one dataset disagree, and what equilibrium models leave out; and how the profession, and now machines, shape what economists find.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: which results replicate?

Your turn. Six results published in the simulated field, each with its design and its test statistic. They were picked by a rule, not for drama: the published significant results at six evenly spaced ranks, from the weakest to the strongest. Two use instruments, one a discontinuity, one a difference in differences, two randomized trials. Their p-values run from four in a hundred down to a few in a million. Each study is now repeated on new data, with a sample big enough to have a ninety percent chance of detecting the published effect, if the published effect is real. Which ones will come back significant, in the same direction? Pause, and write down your six bets.

The results. Four of the six replicated. Study B, an instrumental-variables result with z of 2.27, failed: its true effect was small, a true z of 0.37, and it had cleared the line by luck and by search. Study F is the surprise. Its z was 4.6, the strongest of the six, and its effect is real, a true z of about 2.9. But even a strong published result is usually an overestimate, and the replication was sized for the published effect, not the true one. So the repeat had less power than planned, and came back at 1.70, just short. A replication that fails does not prove the effect is zero, and one that succeeds does not prove the published size.

Now replicate every significant result in the field, not just six. Sort them by the strength of the original evidence. Results just past the line replicate 51 percent of the time: a coin toss. The share rises with the original z, to about 71 percent for z between four and six, but never reaches certainty. These are the field's own odds, and they are the right starting point for anyone reading a new result from it: a p-value of four in a hundred, in a field that searches and selects, is closer to a coin toss than to proof.
Replication: Chapter two. Replication in the lab.

In 2016 a team led by Colin Camerer and Anna Dreber did for experimental economics what the hook did in simulation. They took all eighteen laboratory experiments published in the American Economic Review and the Quarterly Journal of Economics from 2011 to 2014, and ran each again with a plan written down in advance. Every replication had at least a ninety percent chance of detecting the original effect, if it was real. Eleven of the eighteen were significant again, in the same direction: sixty-one percent. And the effects they found were, on average, two thirds the size of the originals. The simulated field of the hook, built before looking, gives 60 percent and 71 percent. Search and selection of the kind it assumes are enough to produce what the laboratories found.

Why are replicated effects smaller? Because publication picks winners. A study is published when its estimate came out high, and an estimate that came out high was, on average, lucky. In the simulated field, where the truth is known, the true effect of a result that barely cleared the line is 62 percent of the published one. For stronger results the exaggeration is smaller, but even above six it is about 20 percent. This is the winner's curse of auctions, Part sixteen, in a new place: the next estimate falls back towards the truth. It is why a failed replication is not proof that the effect is zero, and why an honest replication is sized for an effect smaller than the published one.

Could anyone have said in advance? Called it? Before the replications were run, the team opened a prediction market for each study, and 97 economists traded in them. The average price said there was a 75 percent chance that each result would replicate, and every market was above one half. The outcome: sixty-one percent. And the prices ranked the studies only weakly, a rank correlation of 0.30, not significant; the traders' own answers to a simple survey did better. Partly right: the traders knew the field was imperfect, and erred on the side of optimism. Two years later a similar market on social-science experiments in Nature and Science predicted the replication rate almost exactly. The crowd knew the field was shaky, but not yet which results.
Reproduce: Replication has a ladder, and the words are used loosely, so fix them. To reproduce a result is to get the same numbers from the same data and the same code. To test its robustness is to keep the data and make other reasonable choices. To replicate it is to run the same design on new data, as the laboratories did in chapter two. And to generalize it is to find it in another place and time. Each step can fail for its own reasons. This chapter climbs the first two.

The first rung sounds trivial. It was not. In a 2015 Federal Reserve working paper, Andrew Chang and Phillip Li tried to reproduce sixty-seven papers from thirteen journals. From the posted files alone they managed twenty-two; with the authors' help, twenty-nine of the fifty-nine they could attempt, under half. Most failures were missing files. Since 2018 the American Economic Association has had a data editor, whose team runs each paper's code before it is published. In 2024 the Institute for Replication reported on a hundred and ten recent papers in economics and political science: more than eighty-five percent reproduced from their files, but about a quarter contained coding errors. And when other teams made other reasonable choices, in five and a half thousand re-analyses, about seventy percent kept the original's statistical significance.

The second rung, on a famous case. In Part thirty-two, Thomas Herndon, a graduate student, found a spreadsheet error in Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff's study of public debt and growth. The data are public now, so ask their question many ways. Does growth fall when debt passes a threshold? Try six thresholds, from sixty to a hundred and twenty percent of GDP; average country by country, or count every year once; start in 1946 or in 1950; keep or drop the early postwar years they dropped. Forty-eight analyses, each one defensible, sorted from the most negative gap to the least. The ring marks the analysis closest to their own choices. The grid underneath shows the other choices each analysis made. The threshold, in colour, moves the answer most, then the exclusions; the most negative gap combines the highest threshold, country-by-country averages and their exclusions. 47 of the 48 find slower growth above the threshold. But the gap runs from minus 5.8 points to 0.1, and not one of the forty-eight can say whether debt slows growth or slow growth piles up debt. A robust correlation can still be the wrong answer to a causal question.
Designs: Chapter four. Specification searching by design.

In 2020 Brodeur returned with Nikolai Cook and Anthony Heyes. They collected over twenty-one thousand tests from twenty-five leading journals, and tagged each by the design that produced it: randomized trials, regression discontinuities, difference in differences, instrumental variables. The bunching just past the line was worst for instruments, present for difference in differences, and least for trials and discontinuities. That fits how the designs work. Which instrument, which control group, which time window: these can be chosen after seeing results. A randomization, or a cutoff set by law, is fixed before anyone looks. Edward Leamer had made the general point in 1983, in a paper called Let's Take the Con out of Econometrics: a result that depends on choices nobody reports is not yet evidence.

The simulated field was built with this in mind. Its researchers search more when the design allows it: one in ten after an insignificant trial, three in twenty after a discontinuity, three in ten with a difference in differences, nearly half with an instrument. Journals treat every design alike. In each design's published results, the bump past 1.96 grows from trials to instruments: the caliper ratio runs from 2.9 and 2.9 to 3.2 and 3.6. Fit Andrews and Kasy's selection model, the subject of the next chapter, to each panel. It cannot tell a researcher's search from an editor's rejection, but it measures their joint effect: the share of insignificant results missing from the record rises from 67 percent for trials to 73 percent for instruments. The same journals, different freedom.

And the evidence on the evidence was itself checked. Many papers report coefficients and standard errors rounded to two or three digits, and a z computed from rounded numbers can land just past 1.96 by arithmetic alone. In 2022 Sebastian Kranz and Peter Pütz corrected for rounding: the bunching for difference in differences at five percent faded, while for instruments it remained. Brodeur, Cook and Heyes agreed that this had been their shakiest finding. That exchange is the system working: a claim about bias, replicated, corrected, and narrowed, in the same journal.
Correct: If selection bends a literature, model the selection. That is the idea of Isaiah Andrews and Maximilian Kasy. What gets published is what researchers found, the latent distribution, times the chance that each result is published. In the simplest version, a significant result is always published and an insignificant one with relative probability beta. Beta of one means no selection; beta of a tenth means insignificant results are ten times less likely to appear. The trick is identification. With systematic replications, compare the originals with their repeats, which were not selected. With a meta-study, compare precise studies with imprecise ones: without selection, the imprecise ones should scatter symmetrically around the precise ones.

Here is a meta-study built so the truth is known, shaped like the literature on the minimum wage. 600 published estimates of the elasticity of employment with respect to the minimum wage, each plotted against its precision. Precise studies sit high, imprecise ones low. Without selection this would be a symmetric funnel. It is not. Negative and significant estimates were always published; the rest only three times in ten. In grey, a sample of the studies that were run and never published: the funnel's missing side. The true average elasticity is minus 0.010. The published average is minus 0.017, 70 percent more negative than the truth. Andrews and Kasy's model, fitted only to the published points, gives minus 0.011, and finds that insignificant results were published 31 percent as often as significant ones, close to the thirty percent that was built in.

And on real literatures. On the laboratory experiments of chapter two, Andrews and Kasy estimate that significant results were more than thirty times as likely to be published as insignificant ones. On a meta-study of the minimum wage's effect on employment, negative and significant estimates were about three times as likely to be published, and the corrected average effect is small, about half the naive one. Earlier, Hristos Doucouliagos and Tom Stanley had read sixty-four American studies the same way and found little evidence of any negative effect once selection was removed. John Ioannidis, Stanley and Doucouliagos surveyed a hundred and fifty-nine literatures in economics, sixty-four thousand estimates: the median study had eighteen percent power or less, and nearly four in five reported effects were exaggerated, typically by a factor of two. Corrections are models, though. They assume a form of selection, different forms give different answers, and none can restore the studies that were never run.
Remedies: Chapter six. Remedies: plans, registered reports, many tests.

First, the size of the problem. Suppose nothing is real. A researcher who runs one pre-specified test finds a significant result five times in a hundred: that is what five percent means. But suppose they try several reasonable specifications and report the first that works. If the specifications are moderately alike, five tries give a false positive 17 percent of the time, and twenty give 36 percent. Specifications that differ more raise the rate faster; nearly identical ones barely raise it. Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken called this the garden of forking paths. No one needs to cheat: each choice can be made in good faith, after seeing the data.

The remedy for forking paths is to choose the path before seeing the garden. A pre-analysis plan writes down the outcomes, the sample and the specifications, and registers them, before the data are seen. The American Economic Association has kept a registry for randomized trials since 2013. Benjamin Olken weighed the promises and the perils: plans cannot anticipate everything, they suit trials better than observational work, and they can crowd out the discoveries nobody planned. Registered reports go further. The design is reviewed and accepted before the results exist. The Journal of Development Economics piloted this in 2018, and kept it. What that buys is simple: the result can no longer decide whether the paper is published, so null results enter the record.

A plan also counts the tests. A trial with 10 pre-registered outcomes, three of them truly affected, each with eighty percent power. Test each at five percent and the trial finds 2.4 of the three real effects on average, but 31 percent of the time it also reports at least one false one. Bonferroni's rule, which divides the five percent by the number of tests, cuts that to 3 percent, and finds only 1.5 real effects. Benjamini and Hochberg's rule controls a different thing, the share of discoveries that are false, and sits between: 1.8 real effects, a false one 10 percent of the time. No rule is free; the choice depends on what each kind of mistake costs.
Turn: Step back from single results to the field. Daniel Hamermesh classified every full-length article in the three leading American general journals in one year of each decade from 1963 to 2011. In 1963 half were pure theory and most of the rest used data borrowed from someone else, typically a government. Theory peaked at 58 percent in 1983. By 2011 it was down to 19 percent. What replaced it: studies whose authors built their own data, up from two percent to a third, and experiments, from nothing to 8 percent. The field had turned from proving what must happen to measuring what does.

Why the turn? Partly a complaint. Leamer's 1983 paper argued that econometric results hung on assumptions nobody believed and specifications nobody reported. In 2010 Joshua Angrist and Jörn-Steffen Pischke answered that better research design had taken the con out: randomized trials, and natural experiments like the draft lotteries and minimum-wage borders of Parts four and thirty-eight. Partly the data. Administrative records of taxes, schools, hospitals and firms now cover millions of people rather than the thousands in a survey. That brings a new problem: access to such records is negotiated, often by insiders, and a result that outsiders cannot check is harder to replicate. Chapter three's first rung is hardest to climb where the data are most valuable.
Audit: Chapter eight. Structure, design, and the Dials audited.

The turn left economics with two camps, and this series has worked in both. Design: find variation that is as good as random, a lottery, a border, a cutoff, and estimate one effect cleanly, without saying much beyond the sample. Structure: write down the choices that generate the data, estimate their parameters, and predict the effects of policies never tried. The trade is credibility against reach. The reconciliation, where there is one, is to use a design's clean estimates as targets the model must match, as in Part fifty-four, or to ask the model what a design would have found, as the Island has done all series.

The series kept its own ledger. Every number that a part treated as a measurement of something in the world went into a Dial, with its source and its design. There are now 93 Dials holding 410 estimates, 101 of them computed in these films. By kind: 112 come from designs, trials, instruments, discontinuities, differences in differences and event studies; 90 from structural or calibrated models; 104 from plain regressions. The rest are reviews and meta-analyses, laboratories and surveys, and reconstructions of history. Both camps, and the plain regression that neither camp admires, carry the series about equally: no kind is more than 27 percent of the record.

And how much is settled? Each Dial carries a status, set when its part was written. 20 of the 93 are settled within a range: the evidence agrees about the size. 35 depend on the setting, which is a finding, not a failure: the effect really differs from place to place. 36 are contested, and 2 are not identified at all with the data we have. The widest disagreements: the return to capital in poor countries, where the largest estimate is 63 times the smallest; risk aversion, the neutral interest rate, the productivity effect of AI, and what schools add. These are the questions where the next economics has the most to do.
Analysts: Chapter nine. Many analysts, one dataset.

In 2021 Nick Huntington-Klein and coauthors ran an experiment on economists. They took two published causal studies and gave each to seven experienced researchers, with the original data sources and the question, and let each build the analysis from scratch. No two of the replicators ended with the same number of observations. Their estimates spread three to four times as widely as the standard error each of them reported. For one study, even the sign differed. And most of the choices that drove the differences, how to clean a variable, whom to drop, are the kind no paper reports. A standard error measures sampling noise; it says nothing about the analyst.

The same experiment on a dataset where the truth is known. Four thousand people, a training programme, and earnings afterwards. The programme helps the young most and the old not at all; the young, the poor and some regions enrol more; earnings have heavy tails and a few miscoded records; and three in ten who enrol drop out. Seven analysts each make choices a referee would accept: an age range, whether to drop outliers, how to control for age, income and region, and whether to count everyone who enrolled or only those who finished. Seven sample sizes, seven estimates, from 0.05 to 0.18. Their spread is 2.0 times the standard error they report. Every one of them is defensible. The choices are the uncertainty.

Seven teams sampled seven paths. A computer can walk them all. Every combination of the same choices gives 288 specifications. Sort their estimates from smallest to largest, each with its confidence interval: this is a specification curve. Colour them by one choice, whom to count as treated, and the curve splits: counting everyone who enrolled, including those who quit, dilutes the effect. 97 percent are significant, so the programme's benefit is robust. Its size is not: from 0.03 to 0.20, a factor of 6. The honest report is the whole curve, with the choice that moves it named.

If analysts disagree, ask whether experts can forecast results at all. Stefano DellaVigna and Devin Pope ran an online experiment with nearly ten thousand people and fifteen ways to motivate effort, from piece rates to charity, and asked two hundred and eight experts to forecast each effect first. The experts' average forecast was good, better than ninety-six percent of the individual forecasts: the wisdom of crowds. And credentials did not predict accuracy: citations, academic rank and field made no difference. The practical lesson: collect forecasts before a study. A result is news in proportion to how far it moves what the crowd expected, and a forecast written down cannot be revised after the fact.
Complexity: Chapter ten. What the models leave out.

Most of this series has used equilibrium models. Their critics have a case. The complaint: equilibrium models assume the economy has already settled, that people are alike or average out, and that expectations are right on average. The alternative, argued by Brian Arthur and by Doyne Farmer and Duncan Foley after the crisis of 2008, is to simulate many different agents following rules, and let the aggregate be whatever emerges. Its best case: booms, crashes and fat-tailed swings can come from inside the economy, with no shock from outside, as in the credit cycles of Part thirty-three. Its problem is the mirror image of its freedom: many parameters, many models that fit the same facts, and few ways to estimate or refute them. One model shows both sides.

William Brock and Cars Hommes built it in 1997, on the oldest model of a farm market, the cobweb. Farmers decide how much to plant before they know the price, so supply depends on what they expect. Some pay a cost for the correct forecast; the rest simply expect last period's price, for free. Each period, farmers switch towards whichever rule earned more last time, net of its cost. Beta measures how quickly they switch. And the supply curve is steeper than demand, so a market of naive farmers alone would swing ever wider. Near the steady state the naive rule is good enough and costs nothing; far from it, the correct forecast pays.

Now vary one number, how fast traders switch, and record the prices the market keeps visiting. When they switch slowly, enough of them pay for the correct forecast and the price settles at its steady state. Beyond a beta of 1.9, the steady state loses its stability: the market alternates between a high price and a low one, as traders flood into the free rule when prices are calm and pay for the good one when they swing. Faster still, the cycle splits, and splits again, and the prices become chaotic: never repeating, though nothing outside the market has changed. Fluctuations from nowhere, with every trader acting sensibly. That is the agent-based case in one picture.

And the other side. Chaotic prices can look like random shocks, so the same data fit many values of beta and many other models. This model is small enough to estimate; many agent-based models, with hundreds of rules and parameters, are not. Where the idea has been tested, in laboratory markets, people do switch between simple forecasting rules much as the model says. So the view of this series: agent-based models are a way to explore mechanisms that equilibrium models assume away, like the networks of Part sixty-three and the many agents of Part fifty-two. They earn trust the same way as everything else, by meeting data.
Profession: Who writes economics? Hamermesh's count answers that too, for the same three journals. In 1963, 84 percent of articles had a single author. By 2011, 20 percent did: economics became team work, as the data and the methods grew. Authors grew older: in 1963 half were thirty-five or under, by 2011 a third. And women, weighted by their share of each paper, wrote 4.7 percent of the articles in 1963 and 12.6 percent in 2011. Who asks the questions shapes which questions are asked, and economics has drawn its authors from a narrow slice of the people it studies.

And who decides what is published? In economics, five general journals carry unusual weight: the American Economic Review, Econometrica, the Journal of Political Economy, the Quarterly Journal of Economics and the Review of Economic Studies. James Heckman and Sidharth Moktan followed young economists in leading departments, and found that papers in those five journals raised the rate at which they got tenure, even holding other measures of quality fixed. They called it the tyranny of the top five: many of the most cited papers appear elsewhere, and a few editors' tastes steer careers. It is the publication filter of the first five chapters, seen from the inside.

George Akerlof named a subtler bias. In Sins of Omission and the Practice of Economics, he argued that the profession prizes precise answers, and so prefers the questions that can be answered precisely. Hard over soft: important questions without clean data or tidy models get left aside, and are omitted rather than answered wrongly. And advice is rarely scored. A forecast or a policy claim made on television is seldom put beside what happened. This series has tried to do that in every part: Called it? puts a prediction beside its outcome, the Dials keep the evidence with its spread, and the Facts test the series' own model against the world.
Machine: Chapter twelve. Economics with AI in the loop.

Part sixty-five asked what AI does to the economy. This chapter asks what it does to economics. A research project is a chain: read the literature, build the data, write the code, propose a hypothesis, check the work. Anton Korinek catalogued how language models already help economists at each link, from brainstorming and writing to coding, data and mathematics. Each step gets faster and cheaper, and the errors get more fluent: a made-up reference reads like a real one. The scarce skill moves from doing each step to judging the whole chain.

The most interesting use is the newest: machines that suggest what to test. Jens Ludwig and Sendhil Mullainathan asked what judges respond to when deciding whom to jail before trial. A deep-learning model shown only the defendants' mug shots predicted the judges' decisions far better than chance. To learn what it had found, they morphed faces along the model's predictions and asked people to describe the difference. Two features came out, looking well groomed and looking heavy-faced, neither in the standard lists of what sways judges. Hypotheses found this way must then be tested the old way, on data the search did not use. The machine proposes; the design disposes.

The danger is chapter six at machine speed. With nothing real to find, one test finds something 5 percent of the time; ten specifications, 24 percent; a hundred, 64; a thousand, which a machine can run in a minute, 98 percent. A person tries a few forking paths; a machine can walk them all, and report the one that works. The defences scale too: keep data the search never sees and test there; report the whole specification curve of chapter nine rather than one point; and when a machine's labels stand in for data, correct for its errors with prediction-powered inference, from Part sixty-four.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: how often results replicate.

One new Dial: how often published results replicate. Laboratory economics, the eighteen studies of chapter two: 0.61, with a wide interval because eighteen is few. Social-science experiments in Nature and Science: 0.62. Psychology, in the Open Science Collaboration's hundred studies of 2015: 0.36. And this film's simulated field: 0.60. The status: depends on the setting. The rate is not a constant of nature; it is set by a field's power, its filter on significance and the freedom of its analyses, all of which can be changed.

And the ledger as a whole. Some Dials were opened once and left. Others kept coming back, as new parts met the same number from another side. The most often reopened: the elasticity of intertemporal substitution, the marginal propensity to consume out of a transitory windfall, and relative risk aversion, each in 4 parts. Each reopening added estimates. None has closed a Dial: the range narrows, or the setting is named, but the record stays open. That is what a cumulative science looks like from the inside.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: reading a paper, a forecast, an op-ed.

Four questions for any empirical paper. The design: what variation identifies the effect, and could it have been chosen after seeing the results? The evidence: how far past the line is the key test, how many outcomes and specifications were tried, and was there a plan? The size: is the effect plausible, or is it the size that only a lucky estimate could produce, given the study's power? And what do other studies find? And the record: are the data and code public, and has anyone reproduced or replicated it?

Put numbers on it. A new paper reports an instrumental-variables estimate with a p-value of four in a hundred. In the simulated field, results like it replicate about 51 percent of the time. And their true effects are, on average, about 62 percent of what was published. So a reader's best guess is a smaller effect than the paper's, held with less confidence, until someone replicates it. A pre-registered trial with a p-value below one in a thousand deserves a very different reading. The p-value is the same kind of number; what it means depends on the process that produced it.

The same habits for everything else economists say in public. A forecast should come with an interval, a date and a record: how has this forecaster done before? Part fifty-seven scored the professionals. A model's claim rests on assumptions: which are estimated, which assumed, and would the claim survive a different, reasonable one? An op-ed mixes evidence with values; this series' is-and-ought card separates the two. And when someone tells you what economists know, read the Dial rather than the loudest estimate: settled within a range, depending on the setting, or contested.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: a cumulative record.

The frontier is less a new method than a new habit: keeping the record. Living meta-analyses add each estimate as it is published, with its design and its standard error, and correct the whole for selection. Replication becomes routine, done at scale by institutes and journals, with the failures published too. Results are stored as data, not only as prose, so they can be pooled and checked by machines as well as people. And forecasts are filed before results arrive, and scored after.

This series has kept a small version of that record. Every part entered or reopened its Dials, each estimate stored as data with its source, its design and the date it was checked. 93 Dials and 410 estimates across sixty-seven parts. It is a public good in the sense of Part fifteen: once kept, anyone can use it, add a row, or check one. The next economics will be built less by any single study than by records like this, kept by many hands.
